b1-present-perfect-vs-past-simple.title: Present perfect or past simple?
do: Use the past simple with a finished time: yesterday, ago, last year, in 2019.
Use the present perfect when the time is unfinished or not given: ever, never, yet, so far, today.
dont: Don't say I have seen him yesterday.
Don't use the present simple with since or for to mean up to now: We are married since 2015 is wrong.

questions.q: I ___ (lose) my keys yesterday, so I had to call a locksmith.
a: lost
questions.why: yesterday is a finished time, so use the past simple.

traps.msg: Don't use the present perfect with yesterday, ago or last week.
lose is irregular: lose, lost, lost.

questions.q: I ___ (never / see) snow in my whole life.
a: have never seen
've never seen
questions.why: in my whole life is an unfinished period up to now, so use the present perfect: have never seen.

traps.msg: never saw is informal American English. In exams, life experience up to now takes the present perfect.
After have, use the past participle: seen, not saw.

questions.q: She ___ in Paris for five years, and she still lives there.
questions.why: for + a period that continues now takes the present perfect.

traps.1: lived means she does not live there now. The sentence says she still does.
traps.3: Don't use the present simple for a period up to now. Arabic says أسكن هنا منذ, but English needs has lived.

questions.q: Correct the sentence: I have seen him two days ago.
a: I saw him two days ago.
questions.why: ago always points to a finished time, so use the past simple.

traps.m: i have saw him two days ago
traps.msg: Still wrong: ago needs the past simple, saw, with no have.

questions.q: When ___ to this city?
questions.why: A when question asks for a finished time, so use the past simple.

traps.1: Don't use the present perfect in when questions.
traps.2: A question needs the auxiliary did.
traps.3: do is present, and after do / did the verb is the base form.

questions.q: ___ your homework yet?
questions.why: yet is a present perfect signal in British English and in exams.

traps.1: Did you finish … yet? is common in American English, but exams expect Have you finished … yet?
traps.3: had finished is for a time before another past time. Nothing here needs that.

questions.q: Which sentence is correct?
opts: I went to Turkey last summer.
I have been to Turkey last summer.
I have gone to Turkey last summer.
I was go to Turkey last summer.
questions.why: last summer is finished, so use the past simple: went.

traps.1: last summer is a finished time. Don't use have been with it.
traps.2: have gone also means you are still there. Neither fits last summer.
traps.3: Don't add was before a verb to make the past. كان + فعل doesn't translate word for word.

questions.q: Correct the sentence: We are married since 2015.
a: We have been married since 2015.
We've been married since 2015.
questions.why: since + a starting point needs the present perfect: have been married.

traps.msg: were means the marriage ended. Use have been married.
Still missing the present perfect. Since needs have been.

b1-everyday-phrasal-verbs.title: Everyday phrasal verbs
do: Learn each phrasal verb with a full example sentence.
Put a pronoun between the verb and the particle: pick you up, turn it off.
dont: Don't split three-part verbs: run out of milk, not run out milk.
Don't use to-infinitive after give up: give up smoking, not give up to smoke.

questions.q: We've ___ milk. Can you buy some on the way home? (three words)
a: run out of
questions.why: run out of = to have none left. It needs all three words before a noun.

traps.msg: With a noun after it, you need of: run out of milk.
After have (We've), use the past participle run, not ran.

questions.q: I'll ___ at the station at six.
questions.why: With a pronoun, the particle goes after it: pick you up.

traps.1: Don't put a pronoun after the particle. pick up you is wrong.
traps.3: Without up, pick means choose. That's a different meaning.

questions.q: She ___ her grandmother every weekend because she can't live alone.
questions.why: look after = take care of (يعتني بـ).

traps.1: look for = search (يبحث عن). Arabic speakers mix these up often.
traps.3: look up = find information, for example in a dictionary.

questions.q: He gave up ___ (smoke) two years ago.
a: smoking
questions.why: give up is followed by the -ing form.

traps.msg: Don't use to-infinitive after give up.
You need the -ing form: smoking.

questions.q: Can you ___ what time the film starts? (two words)
a: find out
questions.why: find out = get information you didn't have.

traps.msg: know is a state. find out is the action of getting the information.
After can, use the base form: find out.

questions.q: We ___ at 5 a.m. to avoid the traffic.
questions.why: set off = start a journey.

traps.1: set up = start a business or prepare equipment.
traps.3: came back = returned. You can't avoid traffic by returning at 5 a.m. if you haven't left.

questions.q: Correct the sentence: Put off your coat, it's cold outside.
a: Put on your coat, it's cold outside.
Put your coat on, it's cold outside.
Put on your coat. It's cold outside.
Put your coat on. It's cold outside.
questions.why: put on = start wearing. put off = postpone. take off = remove clothes.

traps.msg: It's cold, so you put your coat on, not take it off.

questions.q: Please ___ this form in capital letters.
questions.why: fill in (UK) / fill out (US) = complete a form.

traps.2: full is an adjective. The verb is fill.
traps.3: feel is a different verb (يشعر). Watch the vowel: fill /ɪ/, feel /iː/.

b1-writing-informal-email.title: Writing an informal email
do: Use contractions: I'm, can't, I've.
Give your reason for writing early, in the first or second line.
dont: Don't use formal phrases with friends: Yours faithfully, I would be grateful if.
Don't translate Arabic greetings: Respected Sam or I wish you are fine.

questions.q: Which opening is right for an email to a friend?
questions.why: Hi + first name is the natural greeting for a friend.

traps.1: This is for a formal letter to someone you don't know.
traps.3: Respected is a translation of المحترم. English greetings don't use it.

questions.q: Which sign-off suits a close friend?
questions.why: Love, / Take care, / Best, are informal sign-offs.

traps.1: Yours faithfully is only for formal letters starting Dear Sir or Madam.
traps.2: Yours sincerely is formal.
traps.3: Don't add from me. The sign-off is followed by your name.

questions.q: Which opening sounds most natural to a British friend?
opts: I hope this email finds you in the best of health.
I hope you are in good health and your family also.
questions.why: Keep it short and natural: How are things? / Hope you're well.

traps.1: Don't use wish for a real hope. wish is for unreal things. Say I hope you're well.
traps.2: This is a translated formula. It sounds very formal to a friend.
traps.3: Translated and too long. Say Hope you and your family are well.

questions.q: Make it informal: I am writing to inform you that I passed my test.
opts: Guess what? I've passed my test!
I hereby inform you that I passed my test.
Please be informed that I passed my test.
It is my pleasure to inform you that I passed my test.
questions.why: Guess what? + contraction + exclamation mark sounds friendly.

traps.1: hereby is legal English.
traps.2: Please be informed is office English, and many native speakers find it cold.

questions.q: Which phrase changes the topic in an informal email?
questions.why: By the way, / Anyway, change topic informally.

traps.1: Furthermore is for essays.
traps.3: With reference to is formal business English.

questions.q: In an informal email you should…
opts: write long paragraphs with no breaks
questions.why: Contractions make an email sound natural and warm.

traps.1: Full forms sound stiff to a friend.
traps.2: Short paragraphs are easier to read.

questions.q: Can't wait to ___ from you! (one word)
a: hear
questions.why: hear from someone = get news from them.

traps.msg: listen is for paying attention to sound. For news, use hear from.
The fixed phrase is hear from you.

questions.q: Which sentence has the best informal reason for writing?
opts: I'm writing to tell you some news!
The purpose of this email is to communicate news.
questions.why: I'm writing to tell you… / I wanted to ask you… are natural.

traps.3: Kindly note is formal office English. Avoid it with friends.

b2-conditionals.title: Conditionals: zero to mixed
do: Choose the conditional by asking: real or unreal? Present, future or past?
Use were for all persons in formal unreal conditionals: If I were you.
dont: Never put will or would in the if clause: If I would know is wrong.
Don't use unless + not: unless already means if not.

questions.q: If she ___ (call) me yesterday, I would have helped.
a: had called
questions.why: Unreal past (third conditional): if + past perfect, would have + past participle.

traps.msg: called is the second conditional, for the present. Yesterday + would have needs had called.
Never use would in the if clause.

questions.q: If I ___ (be) you, I'd apologise.
a: were
questions.why: Giving advice: If I were you. Use were for all persons in exams.

traps.msg: If I was you is spoken English. In exams and writing, use were.
You can never be another person, so this is unreal: use were.

questions.q: Water ___ at 100°C if you heat it.
questions.why: A general truth uses the zero conditional: present + present.

traps.1: would makes it imaginary. This is a scientific fact.
traps.3: Past perfect is for unreal past. A fact is always true.

questions.q: If he hadn't missed the flight, he ___ (be) here now.
a: would be
'd be
questions.why: Past condition, present result (mixed conditional): would + base verb.

traps.msg: now shows a present result, so use would be, not would have been.
will is for real possibilities. This one is unreal.

questions.q: Correct the sentence: If I would have more time, I would learn Japanese.
a: If I had more time, I would learn Japanese.
If I had more time, I'd learn Japanese.
questions.why: Second conditional: if + past simple, would + verb. No would in the if clause.

traps.msg: have makes it a real future possibility. The sentence is imaginary, so use had.

questions.q: Had I known about the meeting, I ___.
questions.why: Had I known = If I had known (inverted third conditional), so use would have + past participle.

traps.1: would come is for an unreal present. Had I known is past.
traps.3: Don't use the past perfect in both clauses.

questions.q: Which sentence is a real future possibility?
opts: If it rains tomorrow, we'll stay home.
If it will rain tomorrow, we stay home.
If it rained tomorrow, we'd have stayed home.
If it had rained, we'd stay home.
questions.why: First conditional: if + present simple, will + verb.

traps.1: Never use will in the if clause, even for the future.
traps.2: rained … would have stayed mixes two patterns that don't fit together.

questions.q: Unless you ___, you'll miss the bus.
questions.why: unless = if not. Unless you hurry = If you don't hurry.

traps.1: Don't double the negative. unless already contains not.
traps.2: No will after unless, just as after if.

questions.q: Should you need any help, ___.
questions.why: Should you… = If you happen to… (a formal first conditional). It is followed by an instruction or will.

traps.1: This is a real possibility, not imaginary, so don't use would.
traps.2: had called is for unreal past. It doesn't fit here.

b2-collocations-work.title: Collocations for work and study
do: Learn the verb with its noun as one unit: meet a deadline, do research.
Use make for results you create and do for tasks.
dont: Don't say make research, catch a deadline, or take attention.
Don't count uncountable nouns: a progress, researches, informations.

questions.q: We need to ___ a decision by Friday.
questions.why: make a decision. In British English, take a decision is also possible.

traps.1: do is for tasks and jobs: do homework, do research. Decisions are made.
traps.2: give a decision is not natural English.

questions.q: We worked all weekend to ___ the deadline.
a: meet
make
questions.why: meet a deadline (or make a deadline) means finish on time.

traps.msg: Don't catch a deadline. You catch a bus.
reach a deadline is not natural. Use meet.
You finish the work, but you meet the deadline.

questions.q: I'm ___ research on solar energy.
questions.why: do / carry out / conduct research.

traps.1: Never make research. This is one of the most common mistakes.
traps.2: As a verb, research has no on: I'm researching solar energy.

questions.q: The manager ___ an important issue at the meeting.
questions.why: raise an issue = mention a problem. raise takes an object.

traps.1: rise has no object: prices rose. You can't rise an issue.
traps.2: An issue can arise (appear), but a person raises it.

questions.q: She ___ a lot of experience working abroad.
questions.why: gain experience. Also: get experience.

traps.1: You win a prize or a game, not experience.
traps.3: You do a job. Experience is gained.

questions.q: Correct the sentence: Please give attention to the instructions.
a: Please pay attention to the instructions.
questions.why: pay attention to is a fixed collocation.

traps.msg: Don't use take. The verb is pay.
The preposition is to: pay attention to.

questions.q: Correct the sentence: You have made a big progress this term.
a: You have made a lot of progress this term.
You have made great progress this term.
You have made good progress this term.
You have made real progress this term.
You have made much progress this term.
You've made a lot of progress this term.
You've made great progress this term.
You've made good progress this term.
You've made real progress this term.
You have made big progress this term.
You have made huge progress this term.
You've made huge progress this term.
questions.why: progress is uncountable: no a, no plural.

traps.msg: Still has a. progress is uncountable.
progress has no plural.

questions.q: Who will ___ responsibility for this project?
questions.why: take / accept responsibility for something.

traps.2: make responsibility is a translation and is not English.
traps.3: do is for tasks, not responsibility.

questions.q: We ___ a team meeting every Monday.
questions.why: hold (or have) a meeting.

traps.1: do a meeting is a translation of نعمل اجتماع. Use hold or have.
traps.2: make a meeting is not natural English.

b2-opinion-essay.title: Writing an opinion essay
do: State your opinion in the introduction and keep it to the end.
Start each body paragraph with a topic sentence.
dont: Don't write Although … but … together.
Don't use According to my opinion. Use In my view or I strongly believe.

questions.q: Where should you first state your opinion?
questions.why: The reader must know your position from the first paragraph.

traps.1: If your opinion appears only at the end, the essay looks unplanned.
traps.3: A neutral essay is a discussion essay, not an opinion essay.

questions.q: Correct the sentence: Although cars are convenient, but they pollute the air.
a: Although cars are convenient, they pollute the air.
Cars are convenient, but they pollute the air.
Even though cars are convenient, they pollute the air.
Though cars are convenient, they pollute the air.
questions.why: Use although OR but, never both in the same sentence.

traps.msg: Remove but. Arabic says رغم أن… لكن, but English uses only one linker.

questions.q: Cars are convenient. ___, they pollute the air.
questions.why: However starts a new sentence and is followed by a comma.

traps.1: Although joins two clauses inside one sentence. It can't link back to the previous sentence like this.
traps.2: Despite needs a noun or -ing: Despite their convenience, …
traps.3: Because shows a reason, not a contrast.

questions.q: Which is the best way to give your opinion in an essay?
questions.why: I strongly believe that / In my view / It seems to me that.

traps.1: For me, I think says the same thing twice (بالنسبة لي، أنا أعتقد). Choose one.
traps.2: According to is for other people's views: according to the report.
traps.3: agree is a verb. I agree, never I am agree.

questions.q: Which linker adds another point?
questions.why: Furthermore / In addition / What is more add points.

traps.1: Nevertheless shows contrast.
traps.2: For instance introduces an example.
traps.3: To sum up starts the conclusion.

questions.q: Correct the sentence: In the other hand, uniforms limit creativity.
a: On the other hand, uniforms limit creativity.
questions.why: The fixed phrase is On the other hand.

traps.msg: The preposition is on, and you need the: On the other hand.

questions.q: Despite ___ expensive, the scheme is worth it.
questions.why: despite + noun or -ing. For a full clause, use although.

traps.1: despite can't be followed by a subject and verb. Use Although it is expensive.
traps.2: It's despite or in spite of. Never despite of.

questions.q: What should the conclusion do?
opts: Restate your opinion in new words and summarise the reasons
Copy the introduction word for word
Change your opinion to look balanced
questions.why: Restate in new words and summarise. No new ideas.

traps.1: Don't add new arguments in the conclusion. Put them in a body paragraph.
traps.3: Changing your position loses marks for consistency.

c1-inversion-for-emphasis.title: Inversion for emphasis
do: Invert the auxiliary and subject after Never, Rarely, Little, Not only, No sooner and Under no circumstances.
Add do / does / did when there is no auxiliary, and use the base verb after it.
dont: With Only when / Only after, don't invert the first clause. Invert the main clause.
Don't invert after Only + a subject: Only Sara knew.

questions.q: I have never been so embarrassed. → Never ___ so embarrassed.
a: have I been
questions.why: Never at the start: auxiliary + subject (have I).

traps.msg: After a negative adverb at the start, invert: have I, not I have.
There's already an auxiliary (have), so you don't need did.

questions.q: He didn't know that he was being followed. → Little ___ that he was being followed.
a: did he know
questions.why: There is no auxiliary in he knew, so add did and use the base verb: did he know.

traps.msg: Little at the start needs inversion: did he know.
After did, use the base form: know.
The order must be auxiliary + subject: did he.

questions.q: No sooner ___ home than she fell asleep.
questions.why: No sooner + had + subject + past participle … than …

traps.1: Missing inversion.
traps.2: No sooner goes with the past perfect, not did.

questions.q: Under no circumstances ___ this door.
questions.why: Under no circumstances + modal + subject + verb.

traps.1: The subject and the modal must change places.
traps.3: Main verbs don't invert in modern English. Use an auxiliary or modal.

questions.q: Only when I left the room ___ my mistake.
questions.why: With Only when / Only after, the inversion is in the main clause.

traps.1: Missing inversion in the main clause.
traps.3: Don't invert the main verb. Use did I + base verb.

questions.q: Correct the sentence: Not only she won the race, but she also broke the record.
a: Not only did she win the race, but she also broke the record.
Not only did she win the race but she also broke the record.
Not only did she win the race, she also broke the record.
questions.why: Not only at the start: did + subject + base verb.

traps.msg: After did, use win, not won.

questions.q: Hardly ___ arrived when it started to rain.
questions.why: Hardly / Scarcely + had + subject + past participle … when …

traps.1: Missing inversion.
traps.2: Hardly … when goes with the past perfect.

questions.q: She rarely complains. → Rarely ___ .
a: does she complain
questions.why: complains has no auxiliary, so add does + base verb.

traps.msg: Rarely at the start needs inversion.
After does, use the base form: complain.

questions.q: Which sentence should NOT use inversion?
opts: Never have I seen such talent.
Seldom do we meet these days.
questions.why: Only + a subject (Only Sara) doesn't trigger inversion. Only adverbial phrases do.

traps.1: Never at the start needs inversion. This one is correct.
traps.2: Only then needs inversion. This one is correct.
traps.3: Seldom needs inversion. This one is correct.

c1-academic-vocabulary.title: Academic vocabulary for essays
do: Learn each word's grammar: facilitate + process, advocate + -ing or a noun.
Check uncountable academic nouns: evidence, research, information.
dont: Don't say facilitate someone to do something.
Don't confuse mitigate (reduce harm) with militate against (work against).

questions.q: The new road will ___ trade between the towns.
questions.why: facilitate = make easier.

traps.1: undermine = weaken. That's the opposite.
traps.2: mitigate is for reducing something bad. Trade isn't bad.
traps.3: constrain = limit. That's the opposite.

questions.q: These results ___ (weaken, C1 word) the original theory.
a: undermine
questions.why: undermine = weaken gradually. results is plural, so there's no -s.

traps.msg: The subject results is plural, so: undermine.
Correct meaning, but the task asks for the C1 word: undermine.

questions.q: Several studies ___ a four-day working week.
questions.why: advocate + noun / -ing = publicly support.

traps.1: Don't add to after advocate.
traps.2: advocate is the verb. Don't add are.
traps.3: advocacy is a noun. You need a verb here.

questions.q: There is a ___ between the two sets of figures.
questions.why: discrepancy = a difference where things should match.

traps.1: notion = an idea.

questions.q: Every investment carries ___ risk.
questions.why: inherent = a natural, permanent part of something.

traps.1: plausible = believable. That doesn't fit a risk.
traps.2: subsequent = later.

questions.q: Correct the sentence: The app facilitates students to learn faster.
a: The app helps students learn faster.
The app helps students to learn faster.
The app enables students to learn faster.
The app facilitates faster learning.
The app allows students to learn faster.
questions.why: facilitate + a process (learning), or help / enable + person + (to) verb.

traps.msg: Don't put the person after facilitate. Its object is the process.

questions.q: Measures were taken to ___ the impact of the flood.
questions.why: mitigate = make something bad less severe.

traps.1: militate against = make something less likely. It's a different word.
traps.3: undermine means weaken something good, not reduce damage.

questions.q: Which sentence is the most academic?
opts: There is substantial evidence for this.
There is loads of proof for this.
There are many evidences for this.
There is a lot of proof about this.
questions.why: substantial evidence: precise, formal, and evidence is uncountable.

traps.1: loads of is informal.
traps.2: evidence is uncountable. evidences is wrong.

questions.q: The data was ___ (= later, formal) analysed by a second team.
a: subsequently
questions.why: subsequently = after that; later (formal).

traps.msg: Correct meaning, but the task asks for the formal word: subsequently.
subsequent is the adjective. You need the adverb.

c1-formal-report.title: Writing a formal report
do: Use headings and the passive to stay impersonal: It was found that…
Make recommendations specific and based on your findings.
dont: Don't use contractions or I think in a report.
Don't repeat the subject: The aim of this report it is to… is wrong.

questions.q: Which sentence is impersonal?
opts: Me and my team asked staff.
questions.why: The passive removes the writer and sounds objective.

traps.1: We makes it personal.
traps.3: Me and my team is also ungrammatical as a subject. Use My team and I.

questions.q: Make it impersonal: We found that the canteen is too small.
a: It was found that the canteen is too small.
It was found that the canteen was too small.
questions.why: It was found that… is the standard impersonal report phrase.

traps.msg: Remove we. Use It was found that…

questions.q: It is recommended that new computers ___ purchased.
questions.why: recommend that + subjunctive (base form): be purchased.

traps.1: Don't use to after that.
traps.2: will is not used after recommend that.

questions.q: Which section suggests specific actions?
questions.why: Recommendations = what should be done, based on the findings.

traps.2: Findings present facts only. Don't mix in advice.

questions.q: Which does NOT belong in a formal report?
opts: Contractions such as don't and it's
questions.why: Contractions are informal. Write do not, it is.

traps.1: Headings are expected in a report.
traps.2: The passive is typical of reports.

questions.q: A significant number of ___ complained about the noise.
questions.why: respondents = people who answered a survey.

traps.1: people is already plural. peoples means nations.

questions.q: Choose the best formal version of: I think we should open the library longer.
opts: It would be advisable to extend the library's opening hours.
I think the library should be open longer.
The library must to open longer.
questions.why: It would be advisable to + precise verb (extend).

traps.1: I think is personal. Reports avoid it.
traps.3: No to after must.

questions.q: The aim of this report ___ to evaluate the new canteen.
questions.why: The aim of this report is to… is the standard opening.

traps.1: Don't repeat the subject with it (الهدف … هو). English has one subject.
traps.2: aim is singular.

c2-cleft-sentences.title: Cleft sentences and fronting
do: Use What … is / was to put the focus at the end.
Use It was … that / who to contrast with something else.
dont: Don't add an extra it: What I need it is is wrong.
Don't use what in an it-cleft: It is the noise what annoys me is wrong.

questions.q: Focus on the noise: The noise annoys me most.
opts: What annoys me most is the noise.
What annoys me most it is the noise.
The thing what annoys me most is the noise.
It is the noise what annoys me most.
questions.why: Wh-cleft: What + clause + is + focus.

traps.1: Don't add it. What … is already has a subject.
traps.2: Use the thing that or what, never the thing what.
traps.3: In it-clefts, use that, not what.

questions.q: We met in 2010. → It was in 2010 ___ we met.
a: that
questions.why: It-cleft pattern: It was + focus + that.

traps.msg: when is heard in speech, but the standard cleft uses that.
Use that after a time phrase in a cleft.

questions.q: Correct the sentence: All I said it was that I was tired.
a: All I said was that I was tired.
questions.why: All + clause + was + focus. No extra it.

traps.msg: Don't put what after All. All I said…

questions.q: She resigned. → What she ___ resign.
questions.why: Focus on an action: What + subject + did + was + (to) base verb.

traps.1: Keep the tenses matching: did … was.
traps.3: done is a participle. You need did.

questions.q: It was Maria ___ sent the email, not Omar.
questions.why: For a person, use who (or that) in an it-cleft.

traps.1: which is for things.
traps.2: Never what in an it-cleft.
traps.3: Maria is the subject of sent, so use who.

questions.q: What does It was Maria who sent it suggest?
opts: Someone thought another person sent it.
questions.why: Clefts imply a contrast or a correction.

traps.2: Clefts are never neutral. Use them only when you mean contrast.

questions.q: The reason why it failed ___ nobody tested it.
questions.why: The reason … is that … Careful writers avoid reason … because.

traps.1: reason … is because says the reason twice. Use is that.
traps.2: The sentence still needs a verb: is.

questions.q: Fronting: ___ as it may seem, I enjoyed the exam.
questions.why: Adjective + as + subject + may seem = Although it may seem strange.

traps.1: This pattern needs the adjective, not the adverb.

c2-idioms-and-nuance.title: Idioms and nuance
do: Keep idioms exactly as they are. Their words are fixed.
Check the register. Many idioms are journalistic or conversational.
dont: Don't translate Arabic idioms word for word into English.
Don't confuse sound-alikes: toe / tow the line, moot / mute point.

questions.q: The policy says it values staff, but nothing has changed. It only pays ___ service to wellbeing.
a: lip
questions.why: pay lip service to = support in words only.

traps.msg: The idiom is fixed: lip service.

questions.q: Online anonymity is ___: it protects activists but also trolls.
questions.why: a double-edged sword = something with both good and bad effects.

traps.1: Don't translate سلاح ذو حدين word for word. Use the fixed idiom.
traps.3: The elephant in the room is a problem nobody mentions.

questions.q: Everyone knew the project was failing, but no one would mention ___.
questions.why: the elephant in the room = an obvious problem nobody talks about.

traps.1: The preposition is in.
traps.2: The articles are fixed: the … the.

questions.q: Whether he knew is a moot point now. This means it…
opts: is debatable or no longer matters
questions.why: moot point = debatable, or no longer relevant.

traps.1: That's mute (silent). The idiom is moot.

questions.q: Ministers are expected to ___ the party line.
questions.why: toe the line = obey, like standing with your toes on a line.

traps.1: tow means pull a vehicle. The spelling is toe.

questions.q: The press ___ with the scandal.
questions.why: have a field day = enjoy an opportunity, often to criticise.

traps.1: A field trip is a school visit.
traps.2: The verb is have, not make.

questions.q: Let's not ___ over the exact wording.
questions.why: split hairs = argue about tiny differences.

traps.1: No article and plural hairs: split hairs.

questions.q: In strict, traditional usage, This begs the question means…
opts: the argument assumes what it is trying to prove
questions.why: Strictly, beg the question = assume the conclusion. In everyday use it also means raise the question. Careful academic writers prefer raises the question for that meaning.

c2-style-and-register.title: Style, register and concision
do: Cut every word that adds nothing: because, not due to the fact that.
Keep a key term the same throughout.
dont: Don't change a key word just to avoid repetition (elegant variation).
Don't mix casual and formal registers in one text.

questions.q: Make it concise: Due to the fact that it was raining, the match was cancelled.
a: Because it was raining, the match was cancelled.
As it was raining, the match was cancelled.
Since it was raining, the match was cancelled.
The match was cancelled because it was raining.
The match was cancelled because of the rain.
The match was rained off.
The match was cancelled due to rain.
Because of the rain, the match was cancelled.
questions.why: due to the fact that → because.

traps.msg: That's the wordy part. Replace it with because.

questions.q: Make it concise: We need to make a decision at this point in time.
a: We need to decide now.
We must decide now.
questions.why: make a decision → decide. at this point in time → now.

traps.msg: Use the verb: decide.
Use one word: now.

questions.q: Formal version: Sales went through the roof.
questions.why: increase dramatically / rise sharply are formal and precise.

traps.1: a lot is neutral or informal.
traps.3: Don't repeat very. Choose a stronger adverb.

questions.q: Concise version: In the event that the system fails, call IT.
opts: If the system fails, call IT.
In case of the event of failure, call IT.
In the event of the system failing, call IT.
Should it be the case that the system fails, call IT.
questions.why: in the event that → if.

traps.2: Still wordy.

questions.q: You called it the policy in paragraph 1. In paragraph 2 you should…
opts: call it the scheme for variety
questions.why: Consistency avoids confusion. Readers assume a new word means a new thing.

traps.1: This is elegant variation. The reader may think the scheme is something different.

questions.q: Which sentence is NEUTRAL in register?
opts: The plan fell apart pretty fast.
The initiative proved unsustainable within a short period.
questions.why: Neutral: plain words, no slang, no heavy formality.

traps.1: pretty fast is casual.
traps.2: This is formal.
traps.3: go belly up is slang.

questions.q: Make it concise: It is important to note that the results were positive.
a: The results were positive.
questions.why: It is important to note that adds nothing. Delete it.

traps.msg: Delete the whole introductory phrase.

questions.q: Why alternate long and short sentences?
opts: To keep the reader alert and land key points
Because exams require exactly half and half
questions.why: Long sentences build an argument. Short ones land it.
